grammar.provenance: unnamed-build-sha-only — two builds are in circulation and are NOT the same artifact (wired 5,961 B / 26 ids; ~/.bb/wasm 5,596 B / 25 ids). The NAMED vocabulary (12) and the field set (2) are identical, so an analyzer matching on type NAMES is immune; a pin comparing named types alone would pass the two as one, which is why the id-order digest is recorded. handled_verified._description: Node types whose construct PRODUCES a symbol or a relationship, or whose result the analyzer CONSULTS before emitting. Re-bucketed 2026-10-17 against the completeness-inventory contract (handled_verified = emits correctly; internal_silent = container/literal/keyword correctly emitting nothing); the historic spec had all twelve named types here, including two whose own prose said they were silent — that was the bucket-as-parking-space defect this round is closing.

_perType.object: a `pair` under an `object` is contained by that object; the SOURCE is the parent SYMBOL's name, never its qualified path
_perType.pair: the key/value unit; a value that is itself an object or array is descended into
_perType.array: a LEAF of scalars but a CONTAINER of objects: an object element is a `class` symbol named `<array>[i]` and is contained by the array
_perType.string: a leaf value; its `string_content` child is the name, never the quoted text
_perType.document: the wrapper; may hold an object, an array, or SEVERAL values (concatenated documents are real input and every one is walked)
_perType.comment: accepted and silent — a JSONC comment is a grammar construct with no identifier to name
_perType.string_content: the declared NAME of a key or a value's text
_perType.ERROR: the parser's recovery NODE, not a construct: the analyzer CONSULTS it to mark a document damaged (damagedFiles) and emits no relationship from it
_perType.MISSING: the parser's INSERT-RECOVERY marker for a missing token: it is damage, never a construct, and correctly emits nothing

internal_silent._description: Node types whose construct is CORRECTLY absorbed with no emission. Each is named with the construct it covers, because a bucket is a ruling, not a place to park something unlooked-at.

_perType.document: the wrapper around one or more top-level values (concatenated documents are real input and every one is WALKED); it names nothing and emits nothing
_perType.string: the QUOTED VALUE wrapper: its name-bearing child is `string_content`; as a bare value it is data carried by its `pair`, and the wrapper itself emits nothing
_perType.number: a literal VALUE node: its text is data carried by its `pair`, not a declaration
_perType.true: a literal VALUE node: data carried by its `pair`, never a name
_perType.false: a literal VALUE node: data carried by its `pair`, never a name
_perType.null: a literal VALUE node: data carried by its `pair`, never a name
_perType.comment: a JSONC `// …` or `/* … */` construct: text with no identifier to name (the historic prose already said 'accepted and silent' while the spec filed it as handled — that contradiction is what this re-bucketing fixes)
_perType.escape_sequence: a `\"` / `\uXXXX` token INSIDE a string: it is spelling, never a symbol, and the emitted value carries the decoded text anyway
_perType.MISSING: the parser's insert-recovery marker for a missing token: damage, never a construct

gap.description: JSON has no names. A key is unique only WITHIN its object, and the store resolves relationship endpoints by name, so 64.54% of the lane's endpoints are ambiguous and 1.97% name no symbol. This is a property of the LANGUAGE, not a defect, and it is NOT closed by a store-side change: measured, name resolves 32.92% uniquely, qualifiedName 5.25%, and EITHER only 34.92% — the two indexes barely compose because `contains` sources are bare names while `references` sources are full paths, so the information is not present in the edge.
gap.status: DECISION FOR THE OWNER — not taken by this lane. Closing it needs the analyzer either to name an ambiguous endpoint by its path or to disambiguate duplicated symbol names after the walk. Measured in reviews/json/m60-closure.md section 7.
gap._denominator: THE APPLICABILITY DENOMINATOR — CURRENT STATE FIRST, then the history this field carried, because two instruments disagreed and only one of them was re-measured. CURRENT (2026-10-09, whole-population census: production `parseFile`, 13,951 admitted files across 154 repos, 0 excluded, 0 repos without a verdict, 0 parse failures): NINE of the ten types are EMITTED — contains 3,990,897 · references 17,117 · uses 9,955 · extends 1,780 · exports 1,200 · calls 263 · implements 113 · imports 82 · overrides 22 — and ONE is excluded, `instantiates` (0 edges over the same population), classed ZERO-SITES, which STAYS IN the denominator. The board row is therefore 9 implemented of 10 applicable: **9/10** — not 8/8, and not 1/10. THE FIRING LOG'S `1/10` IS A TRUE STATEMENT ABOUT 120 FILES, not about json: that instrument samples ONE corpus for this lane (shadcn-svelte — 2,369 admitted `.json` files, measured; the '2,349' this field carried is the corpus-picking comment, not a walk), that corpus is 97.2% `docs/**` theme data, only 25 of its files carry any construct besides `contains`, and the 120-file stride sampled 0 of them; measured WHOLE, the same corpus fires four types (contains 54,575 · uses 339 · references 8 · exports 14). Reconciliation and raw instruments: validation/m14/fixtures/json/measurements/json-firing-reconciliation.jsonl. SUPERSEDED — kept as history, do not quote as current: 'On a deterministic 400-file stride of the WHOLE admitted population (14,009 files across 153 repos) EIGHT labels are applicable and measured: contains 130,787 · references 895 · uses 212 · extends 200 · exports 37 · calls 5 · imports 1 · overrides 1, against implements 0 and instantiates 0 (npx tsx script/m14/incoming-gate.ts json json 400).' design_decision.description: Each construct's ruling, with the evidence that makes it falsifiable. A prose justification alone is not accepted: script/m14/ontology-coverage-gate.ts re-measures every ruling and fails when a ruled type's construct actually occurs.

decisions.question: Which of the 10 relationship types does json emit, and why are the rest inapplicable?
decisions.resolution:
RULED, REVISED FIVE TIMES — the four revisions described below, plus `implements`, which this entry described as excluded until 2026-10-09 and which the whole-population census found EMITTED (113 edges over 1 file; see JSON-G1, now FALSIFIED). CURRENT: NINE are emitted — contains, uses, references, imports, exports, extends, calls, overrides, implements. ONE is excluded, `instantiates`, as ZERO-SITES (0 edges over 13,951 admitted files) rather than by the language. The earlier framing of this line, 'EIGHT are emitted … TWO are excluded by the language: implements and instantiates', is the fourth revision and is superseded. The revisions are the whole content of this entry, because each one was the same mistake. A GRAMMAR INVENTORY says the PARSER cannot express a construct; it does not follow that the LANGUAGE lacks one, because a convention expressed as ordinary object keys is invisible to any grammar. 1) `imports` was ruled out on an inventory ('no import node') and is emitted: a JSON Schema `$ref` is a STRING and the grammar cannot see what a string names. 2) `exports` was ruled out on an inventory ('no export_statement node') — the identical reasoning — and is emitted: a Node manifest publishes through `exports`/`main`/`bin`, which are ordinary keys. 3) `extends` was ruled out TWICE on an inventory, because `allOf` is a KEYWORD and a grammar has no node type for a keyword any more than for a manifest field; it is emitted over 1,432 edges. 4) `calls` was ruled out on an inventory AND on a corpus probe, and the probe was the failure: it searched for `new Foo` command invocations and functions named `new`, i.e. it looked for a JAVASCRIPT-shaped convention and not for the npm one. An npm `scripts` object declares its entries as ordinary keys, so `"pretest": "npm run compile"` invokes a SIBLING script whose name is a key of the same object — both endpoints are symbols in the same file. 215 such invocations across 79 files, emitted. 5) `overrides` was ruled out on the ground that 'a JSON key re-declared in the same object is a duplicate key rather than a redefinition'. Measured, 21 NAMED duplicate keys exist across 11 of 11,713 admitted files, and RFC 8259 §4 says only that names SHOULD be unique and that a parser's behaviour is unpredictable — every mainstream parser keeps the last one, so the second declaration replaces the first. Emitted with the bash lane's edge shape (source = owner symbol, target = the key, `overridesLine` = the prior line), which is the only shape that works when both declarations share one name and one qualified path. What remains excluded — [SUPERSEDED FOR `implements` AND KEPT ONLY AS HISTORY: the census falsified that exclusion (113 `implements` edges over 1 file, pinned by the passing `Inherit.lsp` fixture; JSON-G1). The paragraph below reasons about `implements` as excluded, and its 28-key inventory is the same shape of instrument that missed `imports`, `exports` and `calls` — it searched key spellings in the corpus, and the convention that fires is LSP's `mixins`, which none of its spellings covered. The `instantiates` half of the paragraph STANDS.] On the KEY VOCABULARY rather than the grammar — for JSON the meaningful inventory is which strings appear in the `key` field of a `pair`, since that is where every JSON Schema keyword, manifest field and OpenAPI section name lives. `implements`: the composition keywords are measured on the parse tree — allOf 1,445, oneOf 1,021, anyOf 573, not 206 — and only `allOf` means 'must satisfy all of these', a superset relation, which is why it is `extends` and not `implements`; the alternatives and the negation have no ontology type, and of 28 supertype-candidate keys (`implements`, `inherits`, `superclass`, `base`, `prototype`, `satisfies`, `conformsTo`, …) only `extends` (318), `inherits` (102) and `base` (215) occur at all, and each names a config or manifest field rather than a supertype clause. `instantiates`: 274 keys spell a constructor (`new`, `init`, `constructor`) and NOT ONE denotes an invocation — split by the value's ROLE, they are 142 string values (proxicall's i18n key `new`, nvim-treesitter's `constructor`), 100 array values (duckdb's serialization schemas, where `constructor` is a described C++ field), 22 object values and 10 scalars; and `new <Identifier>` occurs 5,091 times inside strings, of which 7 have that identifier also declared as a key, every example a JS AST dump or a prose message. A probe that matches a SHAPE rather than a ROLE produces a number, and the number is worth nothing. The contrast with bash is the check on all of it: bash emits 7 of 10 on a 164-node-type inventory, json emits 9 of 10 on a 12-named-type inventory (`implements` corrected upward 2026-10-09; the applicable denominator is 10 because `instantiates` stays in). Same ontology, same gate.

decisions.question: JSON has no import statement, so is `imports` inapplicable?
decisions.resolution: RULED: YES it applies, and the first ruling said no — which the ontology gate falsified. The original reasoning was that the grammar has no import node, and that is the WRONG QUESTION: a JSON Schema `$ref` is a STRING, and a grammar cannot see what a string names. Measured over the corpus, 58 `$ref`s across 12 files name another FILE (sigstore/rekor's `v0.0.1/dsse_v0_0_1_schema.json`, for one), and a file-to-file reference is a dependency. So a `$ref` whose value is a relative path ending in a document extension now emits `imports` AND `references`: it is both. A local pointer (`#/a/b`) and a URL are neither — a URL names a VOCABULARY (a JSON-Schema draft identifier), and 38 of the 50 external refs in the corpus are exactly that. Decided structurally, with no regex, so the lane's zero-regex contract holds.

decisions.question: Should a `$ref` edge target the symbol NAME at that location, or the LOCATION?
decisions.resolution: RULED: the LOCATION. Nothing guarantees the name declared at a location is unique — kubernetes/hack/testdata holds two documents in one file that each declare `spec` — while the location itself is. The oracle resolved to the bare name first and disagreed with the analyzer on 7,653 edges, which is 91% of every `references` edge in the corpus; the analyzer was right. Related and the same principle: a JSON Pointer is RELATIVE TO THE DOCUMENT ROOT, so `#/components/schemas/X` names `<module>.components.schemas.X` and not `components/schemas/X`. Looking the raw pointer up against a module-keyed index skipped every kubernetes OpenAPI `$ref` and reported them as fabrications. A pointer is not a path in the document; it is a path FROM the document.

decisions.question: How is an array element identified, and is an array a container or a leaf?
decisions.resolution: RULED: an array element is identified by its index UNDER THE ARRAY, and the array is named by the key it was written under. Deriving the name from the item's PATH by taking the last dot-segment is correct only while the module name contains no dot, and a dotted filename is ordinary: `index.svelte.warnings.json` produced item owners of `warnings` instead of `index.svelte.warnings`, so every `contains` edge from such an item named no symbol. The analyzer AND the oracle had the identical bug, which is the strongest available evidence that it was a shared misreading rather than a slip. An array is a LEAF of scalars and a CONTAINER of objects, so the KIND follows the value's shape: an object is `class` (it has named children and `contains` edges come from it), everything else is `property` — including an array, which the analyzer previously called `variable`, importing a shell-shaped mutable-binding distinction JSON does not have.

decisions.question: What is a symbol's owner, and what is a `contains` edge's source?
decisions.resolution: RULED: the owner is the parent SYMBOL's NAME, never its qualified path. A path is a fine identity and a useless endpoint — the store resolves by name. The original code used the path, which was correct AT THE TOP LEVEL by accident (a top-level key's path prefix is the module name) and wrong one level down, so `inner`'s owner came out as `Basic.nested` while the symbol was named `nested` and the whole top-level corpus agreed with itself. The qualified path is kept in `qualifiedName` and in edge metadata, where it is useful and where nothing has to resolve it.

decisions.question: Does every relationship carry a site line?
decisions.resolution: RULED: yes, and it did not. The string `line_number` occurred ZERO times in the analyzer, so every json edge in the index was stored with a NULL line while symbols carried `range` throughout — the position was known and simply not published. M60 requires a site line on every edge. Now published at all five relationship sites (contains, references, imports, api-endpoint uses, package-dependency uses).

decisions.question: May the analyzer use a regular expression?
decisions.resolution: RULED: no. Zero regex literals, enforced by script/m12/json-contract-probe.ts rather than asserted, and the check scans with comments and strings stripped — the bash lane's equivalent scanner matched its own `/* 0-9 */` comment and the implemented check contradicted its own stated contract. The analyzer also never reads the file as text: every decision comes from the tree, and `node.text` is a tree node's own text rather than the file body.

decisions.question: Are the remaining exclusions sound, or are they the same mistake twice?
decisions.resolution:
RULED, REVISED TWICE — and the second revision is this one, which makes the entry's own history the evidence for it. It originally recorded the remaining exclusions as AUDITED rather than restated, then re-tested each surviving exclusion against the CORPUS for a CONVENTION that would satisfy it. `exports` FAILED that test and is emitted. `extends` was recorded as PASSED and THAT IS FALSE: the audit searched for CLASS-DECLARATION conventions and never searched for SCHEMA-COMPOSITION conventions, so it re-ran the same instrument on the same question and returned the answer it was looking for. `calls` was recorded as PASSED and that is ALSO FALSE, for the same reason one level down: the test looked for `new Foo` invocations and functions named `new`, which is the JavaScript shape of a call. The npm shape — a script invoking a sibling script by name — was never among the conventions imagined, and it carries 215 invocations across 79 files. `overrides` was recorded as unsupplied on the reasoning that a re-declared key is 'a duplicate key rather than a redefinition'; the corpus answers it, 21 named duplicates across 11 files, and a parser that keeps the last one has performed a redefinition. `implements`/`instantiates` PASSED, and this time the pass is a measurement rather than an absence of looking: 3,245 composition-keyword occurrences classified by meaning, and 274 constructor-spelling keys classified by the value's role. — AND `implements` FAILED THAT PASS TOO (corrected 2026-10-09): those 3,245 keywords were counted on a 400-file stride, and the convention that fires is LSP's `mixins`, carried by ONE file in the whole 13,951-file population, where the census counts 113 `implements` edges and the `Inherit.lsp` fixture asserts four of them. This entry is therefore the FIFTH instance of the rule it states, not an exception to it: the instrument looked for composition keywords and constructor spellings and could not have found an interface-mixin convention. `instantiates` stands, and its class is `zero-sites`. The general rule this leaves, now written four times over: an inapplicability ruling is only as strong as the instrument that could have found the construct, and for a convention-bearing language the instrument has to be the CORPUS — read for conventions you did not already have in mind. Every exclusion this lane ever got wrong was an exclusion whose probe could not have found the thing it was ruling on.

decisions.question: Does `allOf` mean a superset-of relationship, and which `$ref` forms does it cover?
decisions.resolution: RULED: YES, and the gate falsified the exclusion twice before the corpus was consulted properly. `allOf` is the only JSON Schema keyword that means 'must satisfy all of these' — `anyOf` and `oneOf` mean ALTERNATIVES, which have no ontology type, and their `$ref`s correctly contribute only `references`. Two ref forms compose, and the corpus has both: `#/…` INSIDE the document, and a SIBLING FILE carrying a fragment (`dataTypeBase.json#`), which is at once an `imports` (it names a file), a `references` (it is a `$ref`) and an `extends` (its role here is composition). Requiring `#/` dropped the file form and reported success, 3 edges short, with every gate green. One form is DECLINED and stated rather than left silent: a bare `#` resolves to the document root, which at the root is the schema itself and so a tautology, and there is one such case in the corpus. Decided from the tree, no regex, so the lane's zero-regex contract holds. Pinned by validation/m14/fixtures/json/AllOf.json, which asserts both composing forms AND the `anyOf` negative, and killed by two mutants: one drops `extends` outright, one narrows it to the intra-document form.
